cards.title: Randomized evasiveness conjecture
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(n_0\ge 2\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\) and every nonconstant monotone graph property \(P\) on n vertices, its randomized adjacency-query complexity with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) satisfies \(R_{1/3}(P)\ge c n^2\)? Both c and \(n_0\) must be independent of P. This card asks for the bounded-error randomized evasiveness conjecture.
cards.why: This conjecture asks whether monotonicity and invariance under vertex names force essentially complete inspection even when random errors are allowed. It is a broad structural lower-bound question covering many graph recognition tasks at once. Its resolution would sharply delimit the power of randomized access to an exact graph property and explain why proximity testing can behave so differently.
cards.status_note: The bounded-error conjecture is explicit in the checked 2002 and 2020 sources and is restated as open in the Winter 2025 notes. Targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. Original model definitions, not informal randomized-complexity labels, govern the reported lower bounds. The search is bounded and cited proofs were not independently verified.
cards.review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-14; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Buhrman and de Wolf explicitly list the bounded-error randomized quadratic lower bound as Open Problem 6 and distinguish it from exact deterministic evasiveness.

Chakrabarti and Khot publish a universal \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) bound for zero-error randomized expected query cost. Its model is stated explicitly here because the informal term randomized complexity can otherwise hide the distinction.

Jain and Zhang extend an influence-based query lower bound to two-sided error and expected query cost. This provides bounds in a model allowing mistakes, without establishing the conjectured universal quadratic rate.
Grossman, Komargodski and Naor separately formulate the bounded-error conjecture in their work on instance complexity; it is not identified with their additional instance-optimality conjecture.
Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal prove the optimal universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query bound for nontrivial monotone graph properties. The theorem concerns quantum query complexity.
Blais’s Winter 2025 course notes continue to state the randomized evasiveness conjecture as open. These notes provide a dated status statement rather than a new lower-bound theorem.

importance.reason: A major longstanding structural conjecture in query complexity, asserting a universal quadratic barrier for randomized recognition across all nontrivial monotone graph properties.

sentences: A monotone graph property is invariant under vertex renaming and cannot be destroyed by adding edges.
The conjecture says every nonconstant such property needs a quadratic number of adjacency queries even with randomized error at most one third.
The query bound is worst-case over graphs and random choices, while the error guarantee holds separately for each graph.
Zero-error expected-cost lower bounds and the solved quantum analogue concern distinct computational models.
A resolution would establish or refute a universal information barrier for randomized exact graph recognition.

cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and let \(E_n\) be the set of unordered pairs of distinct elements of \([n]\). An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) describes a finite simple undirected graph: \(x_e=1\) means e is an edge. Every one of the \(2^{\binom n2}\) assignments is a valid input. A graph property is a function \(P:\{0,1\}^{E_n}\to\{0,1\}\) invariant under every permutation of the vertices, with the permutation acting on each edge’s two endpoints. Monotone means \(x_e\le y_e\) for every e implies \(P(x)\le P(y)\). Nonconstant means some input has value 0 and another has value 1; for monotone P the empty graph has value 0 and the complete graph value 1. No monotonicity across different vertex counts is imposed. A deterministic query tree is a finite binary tree whose internal nodes name edges, whose outgoing branches carry the possible queried bits, and whose leaves carry output bits. On input x it follows the branch specified by each queried \(x_e\). Its cost on x is the number of queries along that path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution \(\mu\), independent of x, on such trees. It has cost at most q if every tree with positive probability has depth at most q. It computes P with error at most \(1/3\) when \(\Pr_{T\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\ge 2/3\) for every input x. Define \(R_{1/3}(P)\) as the smallest such integer q. The distribution and trees may depend on P and n. Sampling, storage and all computation on previously obtained answers are uncharged; only queries revealing one adjacency bit are counted. There is no uniformity or efficient-construction requirement on the trees, and no description of P is part of the queried graph. Queries may be adaptive. Input distributions, promises that a no-instance is far from P, quantum access, certificates and other graph oracles are absent. Cost is worst-case over both the graph and trees in the support, not expected over those choices. The only approximation allowed is the stated probability of an incorrect membership bit. In particular, a graph missing P by a single edge still requires the same success guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed universal lower-bound proposition. A positive answer requires one c and one \(n_0\) working for all the indicated graph properties and all \(n\ge n_0\). Its negation is: for every \(c>0\) and every integer \(N\ge 2\), there exist an integer \(n\ge N\) and a nonconstant monotone graph property P on n vertices with \(R_{1/3}(P)<c n^2\). A refutation must establish this quantified failure, not just a constant-factor saving from querying every edge. A result only for zero-error randomized algorithms, deterministic algorithms, selected properties, or proximity testing does not by itself settle the bounded-error target.

context_blocks.text: Connectedness is monotone: adding edges cannot disconnect a connected graph. It is also independent of how its vertices are named. The conjecture encompasses every property with these two formal features, including properties chosen separately at different graph sizes, rather than only a fixed list of familiar algorithmic problems.

Recognition asks for the actual membership bit on every graph. Property testing changes the required distinction by allowing graphs close to the property to have unconstrained answers. Goldreich’s discussion emphasizes this difference: constant-query proximity testers do not contradict a quadratic lower bound for recognition.

The saved manuscript only briefly describes randomized recognition. This card explicitly adopts the bounded-error convention already used in its working summary, corroborated by Buhrman and de Wolf’s Open Problem 6 and Grossman, Komargodski and Naor’s Conjecture 3.14. The no-error expected-cost question is a distinct weaker variant and is preserved as context, not silently conflated with this target.

For zero-error computation, every sampled deterministic tree is correct on every input and complexity is the largest, over inputs, expected query count. Chakrabarti and Khot prove \(\Omega(n^{4/3}(\log n)^{1/3})\) in that model. Their definition is narrower than algorithms allowed to give a wrong answer. The cited theorem is therefore not itself a proof of the same bound for this card’s larger algorithm class.

The deterministic Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture asks for the exact value \(\binom n2\) for every property at every size. Here the target allows a fixed multiplicative saving and concerns randomized algorithms. A quadratic randomized lower bound would not automatically establish the exact deterministic value. A quadratic deterministic lower bound alone does not exclude randomized savings.

The quantum analogue has a different scale. The 2020 result proves a universal \(\Omega(n)\) quantum-query lower bound, and the property of having at least one edge admits \(O(n)\) quantum queries. Resolving that linear-scale analogue does not resolve the quadratic classical randomized conjecture.

cards.title: Majority outside constant-depth modular circuits
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{MAJ}\notin\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\)? Precisely, for every fixed modulus \(m\geq2\), depth bound \(d\geq1\), constants \(C\geq1\), \(k\geq1\), and \(N\geq1\), is there an input length \(n\geq N\) for which no depth-at-most-\(d\) circuit over AND, OR, NOT and \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\), with at most \(C(n+1)^k\) gates, computes \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}\) exactly?
cards.why: Majority is a basic threshold operation. Showing that constant-depth modular circuits cannot compute it would separate ordinary threshold counting from the full fixed-modulus ACC⁰ model on a simple explicit function.
cards.status_note: The target is explicitly open in Jukna’s source. A 13 September 2026 small-text check of later modular-circuit work identified a symmetry-restricted AND result, not a solution for majority in unrestricted ACC⁰. No resolution was verified; status remains source_open.

progress.text: Research Problem 12.28 explicitly poses Majority outside ACC⁰ after discussing known lower bounds for more complex languages.

The preprint Optimal Lower Bounds for Symmetric Modular Circuits treats AND and syntactically symmetric modular circuits. Its abstract was checked for possible overlap and does not settle unrestricted majority in ACC⁰.

sentences: Majority returns one when at least half of its input bits are one.
ACC⁰ circuits combine Boolean operations and modular-counting gates using constant depth and polynomial size.
The question asks whether every fixed choice of modulus and depth fails to compute majority within polynomial size.
Known results for prime moduli or additional circuit restrictions do not settle the full composite-modulus question.
A separation would show that this shallow modular model cannot express a basic threshold operation efficiently.

cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s Research Problem 12.28 asks whether Majority lies outside ACC⁰. This is a lower bound for one concrete counting function, stronger in explicitness than separating a large uniform complexity class from the circuit class.

Prime-modulus lower bounds and the separation of nondeterministic exponential time from ACC⁰ concern different targets from the full majority question. In particular, results for prime moduli do not cover arbitrary composite moduli such as six.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.

cards.title: Graph nonisomorphism in BPP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that M halts on every binary input x and every random outcome within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions, and outputs the correct membership bit for \(\mathrm{GNI}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each x? The language \(\mathrm{GNI}\) consists of valid encodings of two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs. This asks whether \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\).
cards.why: This asks whether random computation alone can efficiently decide a canonical structural equivalence problem. Nonisomorphism has efficient interactive verification, but the help of an unbounded prover is an additional resource. Settling the BPP question would locate ordinary graph comparison more precisely between efficient deterministic algorithms, randomized algorithms and stronger forms of verification.
cards.status_note: Explicitly open as a BPP question in Goldreich’s April 2017 manuscript. The corrected general upper bound and the full introduction of Neuen’s 2026 survey were checked, alongside targeted later-work searches on 14 September 2026. No verified general BPP algorithm or separation was found. The 2026 deterministic-status statement is not being used as a theorem about BPP, and the bounded search is not an exhaustive proof of current openness.

sentences: Graph nonisomorphism asks whether two graphs have no adjacency-preserving vertex bijection.
The target is one randomized polynomial-time algorithm with error at most one third on every encoded input.
Because BPP is closed under complement, the same question can be phrased for ordinary graph isomorphism.
Interactive proofs, quasipolynomial algorithms and algorithms for restricted graph classes do not provide the required decider.
A resolution would clarify whether random computation alone suffices for this central structural comparison problem.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. At a randomized transition the machine may obtain one independent unbiased random bit, with this transition counted in its runtime. Success probability is over these internal bits for each fixed input, not over a distribution of graphs. BPP consists of binary languages for which such a machine has error at most \(1/3\) on every input and a polynomial worst-case clock over inputs and random outcomes. For \(\mathrm{GNI}\), acceptance is required with probability at least \(2/3\) when the encoding is valid and \(G\not\cong H\); it is at most \(1/3\) for isomorphic pairs and malformed strings. Distinct vertex counts form yes-instances for GNI. The output is only one membership bit, without a nonisomorphism certificate, quantum computation or interaction with another party. One machine and one polynomial must work at all graph sizes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{GNI}\in\mathrm{BPP}\) or \(\mathrm{GNI}\notin\mathrm{BPP}\) in the model above. The positive case must supply one uniform polynomial-time bounded-error decider, or establish its existence, with the required probability bound on every input. The negative case must exclude every such randomized machine. Correctness only on typical graphs, an interactive verification protocol, a method with only expected polynomial time and no suitable clock conversion, or a restricted-model lower bound does not by itself settle this target.

context_blocks.text: Graph nonisomorphism asserts that no bijection of the vertex sets preserves adjacency. An isomorphism is an easily checked witness for the opposite answer; a failed attempt to find one does not certify nonisomorphism. The target requires a bounded probability of error on every graph pair, including highly symmetric instances.

Goldreich’s footnote uses graph nonisomorphism to contrast an interactive proof with a problem not known to have a BPP algorithm. The verifier in such a proof receives messages from a computationally unbounded party. The question here removes that assistance and asks about the verifier’s own randomized computation.

BPP is closed under complement: reversing the answer preserves its error bound and runtime. After checking that the encoding is valid, an algorithm for nonisomorphism can therefore be turned into one for isomorphism, and conversely. Validity checking is needed because both graph languages reject malformed strings. Thus this is exactly the randomized polynomial-time question for ordinary graph isomorphism, with its answer polarity reversed.

The deterministic and randomized targets are related but distinct. A deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider supplies a positive answer here. A negative answer here would exclude a deterministic polynomial-time isomorphism decider and, since isomorphism has efficiently checkable permutation witnesses, would imply P differs from NP. A positive answer here does not automatically derandomize the computation.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.

The general quasipolynomial upper bound also applies to nonisomorphism by reversing a validated input’s answer. Its January 2017 correction matters when interpreting the original arXiv manuscript. Parameterized algorithms and typical-instance performance must separately account for their promises before they can be compared with an all-input polynomial clock.

The 2026 survey concerns the general deterministic frontier and parameterized progress. It does not prove that randomized polynomial-time algorithms are impossible. The BPP question remains a dated source-open question after the bounded later-work check recorded here.

cards.title: Directed reachability in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space
cards.formal:
Is there one deterministic algorithm that decides directed reachability using polynomial time and polylogarithmic working space simultaneously?

Precisely, does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing decider \(M\) and fixed positive integers \(a,k,c\) such that, for every encoded instance \((G,s,t)\) of bit length \(N\), it correctly decides whether \(t\) is reachable from \(s\), while
\[\operatorname{time}_M(G,s,t)\le c(N+2)^a\qquad\text{and}\qquad\operatorname{space}_M(G,s,t)\le c\lceil\log_2(N+2)\rceil^k?\]
Both bounds must hold for the same computation on every input. This is the question whether directed reachability belongs to the class SC.
cards.why: Directed reachability captures nondeterministic logarithmic space and is a basic model of exploring a large state graph. The question asks whether exploration can be both computationally efficient and extremely economical in reusable memory. Its resolution would clarify the relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic space while separating a genuine simultaneous resource bound from two individually achievable guarantees.

sentences: The problem asks for directed reachability to be decided simultaneously in polynomial time and polylogarithmic space.
One uniform deterministic machine must meet both bounds on every explicitly encoded graph and marked vertex pair.
No graph restrictions, randomness, advice or additional catalytic memory are allowed.
Separate efficient-time and small-space algorithms do not satisfy the joint requirement.
The target is equivalently inclusion of nondeterministic logspace in SC, and is weaker than L equaling NL.

cards.definitions:
For an integer \(v\ge1\), the directed graph \(G=([v],E)\) has \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and \(E\subseteq[v]\times[v]\). Loops are allowed, and repeated edges have no separate meaning. The graph may have cycles, arbitrary in- and out-degree and arbitrarily many paths. No planarity, acyclicity, uniqueness, few-path or connectivity promise is imposed. The marked vertices satisfy \(s,t\in[v]\).

Reachability means that for some integer \(\ell\ge0\) there are vertices \(u_0,\ldots,u_\ell\) with \(u_0=s\), \(u_\ell=t\) and \((u_i,u_{i+1})\in E\) for every \(i<\ell\). The zero-edge path makes every vertex reachable from itself. Whenever reachability holds, a path with at most \(v-1\) edges also exists. The required output is one membership bit; a path itself need not be output.

Use the explicit binary encoding \(1^v0\), followed by the \(v^2\) adjacency-matrix bits in row-major order, followed by fixed-width binary encodings of \(s,t\). Each vertex field has \(b_v=\lceil\log_2(v+1)\rceil\) bits and must represent an integer between \(1\) and \(v\). The total length is
\[N=v+1+v^2+2b_v.\]
There are no trailing fields. Any binary string failing this format is rejected. The machine must also meet the same time and space bounds on malformed inputs, measured by their actual length. This representation is polynomially related to the vertex count; it is not a succinct circuit description of an exponentially large graph.

The machine has one two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of ordinary work tapes over fixed finite alphabets, initially blank. Each step changes the finite control, reads or writes a bounded number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell. Time is the total number of steps until its accept/reject halt, in the worst case. Space is the maximum number of work-tape cells ever visited during the run, multiplied by a fixed number of bits sufficient to encode a tape symbol. In particular all counters, indices, remembered input bits and temporary data count toward space. Input storage and the finite control do not count. The single decision bit is the halting state, so no uncharged output tape can be used as working memory.

No random bits, nondeterministic choices, quantum register, oracle, advice, writable input or extra catalytic memory are available. The same finite program and constants work for all graph orders and all valid and malformed inputs. An algorithm may depend on the fixed encoding, but cannot be chosen separately for each graph. The input is read sequentially by its head rather than supplied as a unit-cost adjacency oracle; scanning it is charged to time.

For an ordinary language of binary strings, SC means decidability by a single uniform deterministic machine with a polynomial time bound and a fixed-power logarithmic space bound as above. It differs from merely supplying one polynomial-time algorithm and another polylogarithmic-space algorithm. The exponent \(k\) is allowed to be any fixed positive integer; the target does not specifically demand logarithmic or squared-logarithmic space.

Equivalently, the question is \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq\mathrm{SC}\). Here NL consists of languages decided by a nondeterministic Turing machine with logarithmic charged work space and a fixed polynomial clock on every branch, accepting an input exactly when at least one branch accepts. Directed reachability is NL-complete under deterministic logarithmic-space many-one reductions, and those reductions preserve membership in SC. In particular, \(\mathrm L=\mathrm{NL}\) would imply an affirmative answer, but this card asks only for the weaker simultaneous bounds and does not assert the converse.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the simultaneous-bound existence statement. An affirmative answer must give one exact deterministic decider for all directed graphs and prove its polynomial time and fixed-power logarithmic space bounds with constants independent of the instance. A negative answer must prove that no such decider exists: for every correct uniform decider and every proposed constants, some input violates at least one bound. Separate algorithms meeting separate bounds, a restriction to a special graph family, or a simulation with randomness, advice or catalytic memory is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Exercise 9 explicitly asks whether PATH is in SC and points out that Savitch’s theorem does not settle this. The small-space simulation uses superpolynomial time, while usual graph traversal uses much more than polylogarithmic space.

Barnes, Buss, Ruzzo and Schieber give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with space \(v/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log v})}\). This is sublinear but remains far larger than any fixed power of \(\log v\). Their introduction also separates lower bounds for restricted graph-exploration models from bounds for general Turing computation.

The 2025 paper studies quantum logspace on directed graphs with bounded path counts and reviews deterministic simultaneous bounds for such restricted instances. Its promises and computational model are different from an unrestricted deterministic reachability algorithm.

The February 2026 preprint trades ordinary workspace against an additional tape of catalytic memory. Catalytic storage is extra writable memory that must eventually be restored, and is absent from this card’s model; a small ordinary-workspace bound in that model is not the claimed SC containment.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.

sentences: A language in NP intersect coNP has short efficiently checkable certificates for both yes and no instances.
The question asks whether some such language still lies outside deterministic polynomial time.
Having two kinds of witnesses does not automatically tell an algorithm how to find either one.
The separation would identify difficulty independent of the asymmetric certification typical of NP-complete problems.
The project explores whether efficiently verifiable certainty on both sides can coexist with an intrinsically hard decision process.

cards.definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decided on every input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^k\) steps for fixed constants \(C,k\). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.

context_blocks.text: A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm P\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm P\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.

Specified uniform bit computation and an unconditional language lower bound; excluded confusion with promise and witness-search targets.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits
cards.formal: Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), in the source’s sense \(\mathrm{NP}\), and constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\), such that every unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit computing \(f_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) gates for every \(n\geq n_0\)?
cards.why: Depth-two threshold circuits are a basic model of two layers of weighted Boolean decisions. An exponential lower bound with unrestricted real weights would establish a strong limit on this expressive shallow architecture for an explicitly verifiable computational task.

cards.definitions: A threshold gate on Boolean inputs \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) outputs one if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_i z_i\geq\theta\), where all weights \(w_i\) and the threshold \(\theta\) are arbitrary real numbers of either sign. An unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit on \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) consists of any finite number \(s\) of such gates applied to the original input bits, followed by one threshold output gate applied to their outputs. Arbitrary fan-in, fan-out and length-dependent weights are permitted; omitted inputs can have weight zero. Its size is \(s+1\), the number of threshold gates, not total weight magnitude or the number of bits encoding weights. Constants and direct input-to-output connections can be represented by additional threshold gates, changing size by at most \(n+1\), which does not alter exponential-size existence. Computation must agree with \(f_n\) on every input, with no approximation. The family is explicit in the definition of Section 1.5.1 of the source: there exist a polynomial \(q\) and a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \(f_n(x)=1\) precisely when some binary witness \(y\) with \(|y|\leq q(n)\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). Verifier cost is measured on a standard bit Turing machine. Neither circuit weights nor circuits are required to be uniform or polynomially bounded. The exponential target is interpreted as \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for all sufficiently large input lengths, with one fixed positive exponent coefficient.

context_blocks.text: Research Problem 11.40 asks for an exponential lower bound for unrestricted depth-two threshold circuits. The preceding discussion obtains strong bounds under restrictions on the weights; dropping such restrictions is the point of the question.

The source explicitly defines “explicit” in Section 1.5.1 through polynomial-time verification, corresponding to NP. Requiring the chosen function to lie in P would add a stronger condition that is not imposed here. Counting the existence of hard truth tables without this uniform verification condition would miss the intended explicit lower bound.

Chen’s 2018 paper describes even superpolynomial unrestricted depth-two threshold lower bounds for NEXP as a major frontier and develops conditional implications. Those implications do not supply the unconditional exponential lower bound for an NP family required by this card.

cards.title: Black-Box Hypothesis
cards.formal:
Is every semantic property of Boolean functions that is decidable in randomized polynomial time from a circuit description also decidable in randomized polynomial time from only input-output queries and a circuit-size bound?

More precisely, for every family of total predicates \(F_n:\{0,1\}^{2^n}\to\{0,1\}\), does
\[F\in\mathrm{wbBPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\in\mathrm{bbBPP}\]
hold under the definitions below? The reverse implication follows from polynomial-time circuit evaluation, so this is the usual equality formulation of the Black-Box Hypothesis. The property is defined on every truth table, and a white-box algorithm must be correct for every circuit description of that truth table.

source_formulation.text: The main statement, which we will call here ‘the Black-Box Hypothesis’, remains open.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 4

cards.why: The hypothesis asks whether reading an efficient program can reveal any efficiently decidable fact about its function that could not also be learned efficiently by running the function on selected inputs. It connects the limits of program analysis with circuit complexity and obfuscation. Its truth would imply that NP is not contained in BPP, while restricted failures have known consequences for the complexity of circuit satisfiability.

Conditional consequences quoted from these sources were checked for scope, not independently reproved.

sentences: The Black-Box Hypothesis compares access to a Boolean circuit’s code with access to its input-output behavior.
It concerns total semantic properties that a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm decides correctly on every circuit representation.
The proposed black-box algorithm receives unary input length and circuit-size bounds and may make adaptive evaluations of the function.

cards.definitions:
For each integer \(n\ge0\), a Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) has the length-\(2^n\) truth table \(\operatorname{tt}(f)\), ordered lexicographically by input. A property is an arbitrary family \(F=(F_n)_{n\ge0}\) of total Boolean predicates on these tables. It need not be invariant under permutations of the input variables or table positions. Its semantic character means that two circuits computing the same \(n\)-input function have the same required property value.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with designated input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. Wires may share gate outputs; unrestricted depth is allowed. Unused designated input vertices are retained. Its size \(s(C)\) is the number of vertices plus wires, and its computed function is \(f_C\). Define \(s(f)=\min\{s(C):f_C=f\}\). Counting input vertices is a harmless explicit convention because the black-box resource bound includes \(n\).

Descriptions list all vertices in topological order, their types and earlier incoming indices, followed by the output index; integers use self-delimiting binary fields. This gives a polynomial-time parsable encoding of length polynomial in \(s(C)+1\), including all \(n\) input vertices. Any fixed encoding with these properties gives the same polynomial-time target. Malformed descriptions are rejected.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{wbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(c,k\) such that \(A\) halts on every input and every random-bit sequence within \(c(N+1)^k\) steps, where \(N\) is description length, and
\[\forall C,\qquad \Pr[A(\operatorname{desc}(C))=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f_C))]\ge2/3.\]
The same machine must work across all sizes and arities and on every representation of a function, including padded or redundant circuits. The acceptance probabilities for different representations need not be equal; each must give the correct Boolean property value with the stated error bound.

A property belongs to \(\mathrm{bbBPP}\) if there are one uniform probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(B\) and fixed positive integers \(d,\ell\) such that \(B^f(1^n,1^m)\) halts within \(d(n+m+1)^\ell\) steps on every random-bit sequence, and
\[\forall n\ge0\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\ \forall m\ge1,\quad m\ge s(f)\ \Longrightarrow\ \Pr[B^f(1^n,1^m)=F_n(\operatorname{tt}(f))]\ge2/3.\]
Here \(m\) is an integer upper bound, not necessarily the minimum circuit size. Both parameters are in unary. A query consists of an explicitly written \(n\)-bit string \(x\); the oracle returns \(f(x)\) in one step. Writing and manipulating the query counts toward time. Invalid-length queries return a fixed zero bit. Queries may be adaptive, and all computation between queries also counts. Thus the bound is on running time, not merely the number of oracle calls. The same machine and polynomial work for all valid bounds \(m\). If \(m<s(f)\), no correctness is required, but the running-time bound remains.

Both machines use independent fair random bits, and all probabilities above are over those bits for each fixed input or oracle. They have no advice or other oracle. In the black-box case, \(f\) and the unary parameters are the only supplied information about the function; no circuit, truth table, distribution on circuits or special representation is given. The circuit-size promise in this definition does not turn \(F_n\) into a partial property: \(F_n\) is defined on every Boolean function.

The quantifiers allow \(A,B\) and their polynomial constants to depend on \(F\). The conclusion is existence of a suitable \(B\) for every white-box decidable property, not an additional requirement of an effective procedure that transforms arbitrary machine descriptions into black-box algorithms.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the universal implication. A proof must establish a uniform black-box algorithm with the stated total running-time and pointwise error guarantees for every total semantic property in white-box BPP. A refutation must specify one such property and a correct white-box BPP algorithm and prove that no black-box BPP algorithm decides it under the supplied-size-bound model. A property defined only on a promised family of circuits, a distinction between two encodings of the same function, or a lower bound only for nonadaptive queries does not alone meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2017 source identifies this as the total-property form of the scaled-down Rice’s theorem conjecture originating in work on program obfuscation. It distinguishes the still-open hypothesis from conditional counterexamples to a promise version; those counterexamples do not decide a property on every circuit.

The authors prove consequences of particular kinds of hypothetical counterexamples, including ones with highly sensitive low-complexity functions. These are conditional implications for circuit satisfiability, rather than a general proof or disproof of the hypothesis.

The 2021 paper retains the original hypothesis as open and studies other combinations of analysts and represented computations. Its positive results for restricted circuit analysts, and its equivalence involving nondeterministic circuits as boxes, change the computational models and do not settle ordinary circuits with uniform BPP analysts.

The cost of black-box computation includes the unary circuit-size bound. This avoids demanding a polynomial-in-arity algorithm for properties of functions whose smallest circuits are already exponentially large, and makes the two kinds of access comparable.

cards.definitions: An MCSP input is the complete truth table \(t\in \{0,1\}^{2^{n}}\) of a Boolean function on \(n\ge 1\) input bits, in lexicographic order, together with a nonnegative integer size threshold s in binary. It is accepted if some Boolean circuit of size at most s computes that function. Circuits are finite acyclic graphs over binary AND and OR, unary NOT, input variables and constants 0,1, with one designated output and unrestricted sharing. Size counts noninput gates, including constant gates. The total encoded input length counts the truth table, threshold and delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. NP-hardness means that for every language L in NP there is a deterministic polynomial-time map r such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(r(x)\in\)MCSP. NP consists of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup _{k\ge 1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{k}}); \mathrm{P}\)/poly consists of languages decided by families of Boolean circuits whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in input length, with no uniformity condition on their construction. \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly means that some language in EXP has no such polynomial-size circuit family.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the conditional implication or its logical negation in these exact reduction and circuit models. Deriving only \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\) or \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly is a weaker consequence. A theorem for a restricted reduction class or for partial, promise or approximate circuit minimization does not prove the stated implication.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?

cards.definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b- 1; a\) terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(\mathrm{P}(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.title: A steady stream of digits
context_blocks.text: For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

context_blocks.title: The finite description is not the resource bound
context_blocks.text: The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

context_blocks.title: Why sources also say linear time
context_blocks.text: Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

context_blocks.title: What the partial results establish
context_blocks.text: Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The input representation matters
context_blocks.text: The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

cards.title: Nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) perfect matching
cards.formal:
Does perfect-matching decision for general undirected graphs have nonuniform Boolean circuits of polynomial size and logarithmic depth?

For each integer \(v\ge2\), let \(\mathrm{PM}_v:\{0,1\}^{\binom v2}\to\{0,1\}\) indicate whether the encoded graph has a perfect matching. The target is the existence of fixed positive integers \(a,b,d\) and circuits \((C_v)_{v\ge2}\) such that
\[\forall v\ge2,\quad |C_v|\le a(v+1)^b,\qquad\operatorname{depth}(C_v)\le d\lceil\log_2(v+2)\rceil,\]
\[\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\binom v2},\qquad C_v(x)=\mathrm{PM}_v(x).\]
The gates have fan-in at most two, and negation is allowed. The circuits need not be generated uniformly, and the output is only the decision bit.
cards.why: Perfect matching is a central polynomial-time graph problem whose exact bounded-fan-in depth remains poorly understood. A negative answer would separate nonuniform NC-one from P/poly using a concrete polynomial-time task. A positive answer would put the decision problem at a much shallower level than the broad polylogarithmic-depth parallel algorithms studied in most matching work.

cards.definitions:
A graph has vertex set \([v]=\{1,\ldots,v\}\) and an arbitrary set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices as edges. It is simple, undirected and unweighted, with no promise of bipartiteness, planarity, bounded degree or a matching already known to exist. Its input bits are \(x_{ij}\) for \(1\le i<j\le v\), in lexicographic order; \(x_{ij}=1\) precisely when the edge is present. Every bit string of this length is a valid graph. The input length \(m=\binom v2\) is polynomially related to \(v\), so the polynomial-size and logarithmic-depth requirements have the same meaning with either parameter. The statement starts at \(v=2\); the fixed zero- and one-vertex cases do not affect the asymptotic question.

A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share a vertex. It is perfect if every vertex belongs to exactly one selected edge. Consequently \(\mathrm{PM}_v=0\) for odd \(v\). The algorithmic target is to output one bit indicating existence, not to construct a matching, count matchings or decide a weighted exact-value variant.

A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with variable inputs, constants \(0,1\), binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output. A gate output can feed arbitrarily many later gates. The size \(|C|\) is the number of computational gates, and depth is the maximum number of such gates on a path to the output. Variable and constant inputs have depth zero and do not count toward size. Input handling here is entirely through the indicated input wires; no oracle, random bits, threshold gates or unbounded-fan-in AND/OR primitives are present. Correctness is exact on every assignment.

Nonuniform means that each \(C_v\) may be chosen independently; there is no computability, logspace generation or polynomial-time construction requirement on the sequence. The integers \(a,b,d\) must nevertheless be fixed across all graph orders. This is the usual nonuniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) target. A circuit satisfying the logarithmic depth bound can be expanded into a tree of polynomial size, so the simultaneous size requirement causes no additional asymptotic restriction in this single-output bounded-fan-in setting.

Equivalently, \(\mathrm{PM}_v\) must have polynomial-size De Morgan formulas. Such a formula is a rooted tree of binary AND/OR gates with possibly negated variable leaves; each repeated occurrence of a variable is counted separately, and internal values cannot be shared. Formula balancing yields logarithmic depth from polynomial leaf size. A negative answer is failure of every polynomial formula bound for this fixed family, or equivalently that its minimum circuit depth is not \(O(\log v)\); a lower bound may be witnessed at arbitrarily large graph orders rather than at every order.

For source fidelity, the draft’s function \(\mathrm{Match}_v\) asks whether the maximum matching size is at least \(v/3+1\), interpreted as the integer threshold \(k_v=\lceil v/3+1\rceil\). The two decision families are equivalent for the present circuit class. To express a size-at-least-\(k\) question as perfect matching, when \(0\le k\le v/2\), add \(v-2k\) new vertices adjacent to every original vertex and to no new vertex. The enlarged graph has a perfect matching exactly when the original graph has a matching of size at least \(k\). Thresholds above \(\lfloor v/2\rfloor\) are constantly false. Conversely, for a graph on \(2q\) vertices with \(q\ge3\), adding \(q-3\) isolated vertices makes the source threshold \((3q-3)/3+1=q\), so its Match answer is exactly the original perfect-matching answer. Smaller graph orders and odd perfect-matching orders have fixed finite answers. cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\), the function \(S_{n}:\{0,1,2\}^{n}\to \{0,1,2\}^{n}\) that removes all symbols 2 and appends the same number of 2s on the right, preserving the order of the other symbols, is computed by a Boolean circuit with at most Cn gates in the model below?
cards.definitions: Encode symbols 0,1,2 as 00,01,10 respectively. The circuit has 2n input bits and 2n output bits, with arbitrary fan-out, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and optional Boolean constant gates. Size counts all non-input gates, including constants; wires and output designations cost nothing. Correctness is required only on concatenations of the three valid encodings; output on inputs containing 11 is unrestricted. If \(i_{1}<\ldots <i_{m}\) are exactly the indices with \(a_{i}\ne 2\), the required decoded output is \(a_{i_{1}}\ldots a_{i_{m}}\) followed by \(n- m\) copies of 2. In particular, 0s and 1s retain their relative order. The circuit may depend on n; no uniform construction algorithm, depth bound, monotonicity restriction or indivisible-record model is imposed. The constant C is independent of n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.

cards.title: KRW formula-size conjecture with constant loss
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(\alpha>0\) such that for every pair of positive integers \(n,m\) and every pair of nonconstant total Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), \(g:\{0,1\}^m\to\{0,1\}\),
\[L(g\circ f)\ge\alpha L(g)L(f)?\]
Here \((g\circ f)(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)})=g(f(x^{(1)}),\ldots,f(x^{(m)}))\) on \(m\) disjoint \(n\)-bit blocks, and \(L\) is minimum De Morgan formula leaf size. The constant is chosen before all dimensions and functions.

This card retains the constant-factor formula-size version displayed as Conjecture 5.13 in the source book. It is stronger than versions permitting a growing multiplicative loss. The original KRW paper formulates a depth-composition question; the card does not identify that question, weakened quantitative versions, and the displayed constant-loss formula statement as equivalent.
cards.why: A formula for a composition can substitute an inner computation wherever an outer input is used, multiplying the leaf counts. A universal matching lower bound would show that alternative Boolean factorizations cannot save more than a constant factor on arbitrary block compositions. This is a strong structural statement about formulas, closely connected to the source’s superpolynomial formula lower-bound question.

A bounded later-work search did not identify a proof or refutation of this exact all-function constant-loss formula-size version. Its strong quantitative choice follows the book’s display and is distinguished from the original depth question and relaxed KRW variants. The source-open label is limited by this formulation-specific literature review.

importance.reason: A structural conjecture about formula composition that could turn local lower bounds into stronger general formula lower bounds.

sentences: The selected KRW variant asks whether minimum formula size under block composition is always within a constant factor of the product of the two minimum sizes.
Both functions can be arbitrary nonconstant Boolean functions, and the inner one is applied to disjoint input blocks.
Formulas use binary AND and OR with negation, count variable occurrences, and cannot share intermediate computations.
The constant must work for every function and dimension, so dimension-dependent losses do not suffice.
The original depth conjecture and recent results for strengthened communication tasks are related but distinct statements.

cards.definitions:
For a positive integer \(r\), a total Boolean function is a map \(h:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\). Nonconstant means that it takes both values on its domain; it need not depend on every designated input coordinate. A De Morgan formula for \(h\) is a finite rooted tree whose internal operations are binary AND, binary OR, and unary NOT, and whose leaves are input variables or the constant bits zero and one. Its value is obtained by the usual Boolean operations from leaves to the root. It must compute \(h\) exactly on every input, with no randomness or promise on input values. There are no parity, threshold, arbitrary truth-table or unbounded-fan-in gates.

Formula size is the number of occurrences of input variables among its leaves. Positive and negated occurrences both count, and different occurrences of the same variable count separately. Constant leaves are free and can be eliminated from an optimum for a nonconstant function. NOT operations can be pushed onto variables without changing this measure. The minimum over all such formulas is \(L(h)\); it is a finite positive integer for nonconstant \(h\). No internal value can be shared between two parent operations: such reuse would produce a circuit rather than a formula.

The composed function has exactly \(mn\) designated coordinates \(x^{(j)}_i\), with \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Block coordinates are distinct and unconstrained. The same inner function \(f\) is applied to every block, and its outputs, in block order, become the inputs of \(g\). The composition symbol here means this block operation, not ordinary composition of two maps with the same domain. Both functions and their composition may be specified by arbitrary finite truth tables, and no uniformity, polynomial-time evaluability, or monotonicity is assumed.

Since both functions are nonconstant, every Boolean vector supplied to \(g\) can be realized by some collection of blocks, and the composition is nonconstant. The usual substitution bound gives \(L(g\circ f)\le L(g)L(f)\). The question is whether the ratio to that upper bound is bounded away from zero uniformly over all functions and dimensions. Equivalently, is the infimum of these positive ratios strictly positive? This infimum need not be attained. Restricting \(0<\alpha\le1\) is equivalent.

The negation says that for every positive \(\alpha\), some pair and dimensions have ratio smaller than \(\alpha\). Thus a single saving relative to exact multiplication, or even failure of one proposed constant, is insufficient to refute the claim. Allowing constant functions with the convention \(L(h)=0\) would add only trivial inequalities; their exclusion makes the ratio formulation well-defined. Minimum depth, which counts gates along a longest path, is a different measure from the number of leaves.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the constant-loss formula-size statement. A positive answer must establish one strictly positive factor for every permitted pair and dimensions. A negative answer must establish ratios arbitrarily close to zero, not merely a finite violation of equality or an unbounded additive saving in formula depth. Bounds for almost all functions, for special inner functions, for monotone formulas, or for a stronger communication search task do not alone prove the all-function claim. A composition inequality with a loss depending on either dimension, even polylogarithmically, is a weaker result unless upgraded to the fixed constant required here.

context_blocks.text: The book displays an absolute multiplicative constant in Conjecture 5.13. Its accompanying footnote also permits investigation of weaker losses and typical-function variants. The title and acceptance criterion identify which of those possibilities this record actually asks for.

The 1995 paper’s Open Question 4.1 asks about depth under composition and records examples with a growing additive loss in that measure. Those depth examples are not, by themselves, counterexamples to a constant-factor statement about minimum formula leaf count. The original paper and the later size formulation must be distinguished.

The 2023 paper explicitly distinguishes the original depth conjecture from the formula-size variant. Its Theorem 8.1 and Corollary 8.2 prove composition bounds involving a separate inner-function complexity measure and dimension-dependent losses. Those theorems give important restricted comparisons without supplying the universal constant asserted in this card.

The 2025 STACS result concerns strong composition of communication relations: in addition to finding a differing input bit, the answer must lie in a block where the two inner-function outputs differ. That added requirement makes a different search task. The paper explicitly says its lower bounds do not directly translate into ordinary formula-depth lower bounds, and they also do not establish the present size inequality.

cards.title: Closure of UL under complement
cards.formal:
Is unambiguous logarithmic space closed under Boolean complement?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^*,\qquad L\in\mathrm{UL}\ \Longrightarrow\ \{0,1\}^*\setminus L\in\mathrm{UL}.\]
Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{coUL}\)? A language is in \(\mathrm{UL}\) if one uniform nondeterministic machine decides it using logarithmic work space and has at most one accepting computation path on every input.

The complementing machine must also have at most one accepting path on every input and logarithmic space with its own fixed constants. The question concerns ordinary uniform machines with no advice or oracle and arbitrary binary input languages, not only planar graph problems.

source_formulation.text: Thus it is far less clear what it should mean to say that a function is “computable in UL” since it remains an open question […]

cards.why: Unambiguity retains existential computation while limiting each positive instance to a unique accepting history. Complement closure asks whether the same economy is available for negative instances. Its resolution would clarify a basic structural property between deterministic and nondeterministic logarithmic space and the interpretation and composition of functions computed using unambiguous subroutines.

sentences: UL contains languages decided with logarithmic work space and at most one accepting computation path per input.
The question asks whether the complement of every such language also has an unambiguous logarithmic-space decider.
The original and complement machines are uniform, exact and have no oracle or nonuniform advice.

A resolution would clarify both the structure of small-space complexity classes and the use of unambiguous subroutines in graph algorithms.

cards.definitions:
A language is any set of finite binary strings, and \(n=|x|\) denotes input length. Use a nondeterministic multitape Turing machine with fixed finite control and fixed finite tape alphabets, a two-way read-only input tape with end markers, and finitely many initially blank work tapes. Each transition has at most two choices. The input cannot be modified or used as additional writable memory. Work space is the total number of work-tape cells visited along a computation, measured in bits up to the fixed alphabet factor; the input cells and fixed finite control are not charged as work space.

A machine is logarithmic-space bounded if there is a constant \(c\) such that every computation on every input of length \(n\) visits at most \(c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) work cells. Use the standard halting convention: some fixed polynomial \(K(n+2)^d\) bounds the number of steps along every computation path, including rejecting paths. The machine and \(c,K,d\) are fixed independently of the input. A polynomial clock fits in logarithmic space; this convention does not add a nonuniform resource.

A computation path is a complete sequence of transition choices from the initial configuration to an accepting or rejecting halt. Distinct choice histories count as distinct paths even when they later reach the same configuration. Acceptance means that at least one path accepts. The machine decides \(L\) when it accepts exactly the strings of \(L\); all paths on strings outside \(L\) reject.

Unambiguity means at most one accepting path for every binary input. Therefore a yes-instance has exactly one accepting path, while a no-instance has none. There may be many rejecting paths in either case. No probability distribution or bounded-error interpretation of these paths is intended. This is not the stronger requirement that every configuration, or every pair of configurations, be connected by at most one path.

The class \(\mathrm{UL}\) consists of languages decided by some machine satisfying all these conditions. Define \(\mathrm{coUL}=\{\overline L:L\in\mathrm{UL}\}\), where \(\overline L=\{0,1\}^*\setminus L\). Dropping only the unambiguity restriction gives \(\mathrm{NL}\), and restricting to deterministic transitions gives \(\mathrm L\). The usual inclusions are \(\mathrm L\subseteq\mathrm{UL}\subseteq\mathrm{NL}\). The known closure \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) makes \(\mathrm{UL}=\mathrm{NL}\) sufficient for the requested closure; no equivalence to that stronger equality is asserted.

The quantifier is over languages: for each language with a qualifying machine, another qualifying machine for its complement must exist. An effective compiler that transforms every description of an unambiguous machine into a complement machine is not additionally required. Nor must the original and complement machines have the same space constant or polynomial clock. A negative answer is a language in \(\mathrm{UL}\) whose complement is not in \(\mathrm{UL}\), with nonmembership excluding all possible unambiguous logarithmic-space machines.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of closure in the declared uniform model. A proof must establish a qualifying complement machine for every language in UL, with exact acceptance, unambiguity on all inputs and logarithmic work space. A refutation must establish a language in UL and prove that its complement has no such machine. Merely complementing nondeterministic logspace while allowing multiple accepting paths, adding advice or an oracle, or settling a restricted family of graph inputs does not meet the full criterion. An oracle separation or a conditional separation alone is not an unconditional refutation.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
cards.formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants \(c_{M} \ge  1\) and an integer \(d_{M} \ge  1\) so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair \((x,M(x))\), uses at most \(c_{M} S_{M}(x)\) tape cells, and takes at most \(c_{M} T_{M}(x)^{d_{M}}\) steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here \(S_{M}\) counts total storage including input and output, and \(T_{M}\) is at least the input length, as defined below.
cards.definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. \(S_{M}(x)\) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. \(T_{M}(x)\) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and \(M(x)\), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

cards.title: \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\) versus MA
cards.formal:
Do the following two classes of ordinary decision languages coincide?
\[\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{MA}.\]
An \(\mathrm{MA}\) language has a polynomial-length classical witness and a polynomial-time randomized verifier: a yes-instance has some witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\), and every witness to a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\).

For \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\), the witness predicate must additionally be an ordinary BPP language on pairs. Its acceptance probability is therefore always at most \(1/3\) or at least \(2/3\), including for every unsuccessful witness on a yes-instance. The equality asks whether every MA language admits some verifier with that stronger all-pairs gap, possibly with a different witness encoding and polynomial length bound.
cards.why: Existential witnesses and randomized verification interact differently depending on whether every witness must induce a valid bounded-error decision. Resolving this equality would determine whether the additional gap requirement changes computational power or only the presentation of a verifier. The distinction is fundamental when probabilistic predicates are nested beneath quantifiers in classical and quantum complexity hierarchies.

cards.definitions:
A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\). Use uniform finite-program probabilistic multitape Turing machines, with independent fair random bits, binary input and an accept/reject output. Every random-bit sequence must lead to a halt in time polynomial in input length. Bit operations, random-bit generation and input and output handling count as work. No advice, oracle or quantum register is supplied.

For definiteness, encode a pair by \(\langle x,y\rangle=1^{|x|}0xy\). The initial unary field specifies exactly how many subsequent bits form \(x\), and the rest form \(y\). Strings without such a complete parse are malformed; a pair verifier rejects them deterministically. This is a uniquely decodable, polynomial-size encoding. On well-formed pairs, the time bound is at most \(C(|x|+|y|+2)^d\) for fixed positive integers \(C,d\), and the usual polynomial bound applies to all encoded inputs. Let \(a_V(x,y)=\Pr[V(\langle x,y\rangle)=1]\).

The class \(\mathrm{MA}\) consists of languages \(L\) for which there are a verifier \(V\) as above and fixed positive integers \(c,k\), giving a witness bound \(p(n)=c(n+1)^k\), such that
\[x\in L\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \text{and}\ a_V(x,y)\ge2/3,\]
\[x\notin L\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall y,\ |y|\le p(|x|)\ \Longrightarrow\ a_V(x,y)\le1/3.\]
The witness is chosen before the verifier's random bits are drawn, so it cannot depend on their realized values. When \(x\in L\), the probabilities for other witnesses may be anywhere in \([0,1]\). The language is total as a decision problem: every input is either in \(L\) or in its complement; this is not a promise-MA problem with unclassified inputs.

A language \(A\) is in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) if some uniform randomized polynomial-time machine accepts each \(z\in A\) with probability at least \(2/3\) and each \(z\notin A\) with probability at most \(1/3\). In particular, every input has the required gap. Define the existential operator by
\[L\in\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists A\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \exists c,k\ge1\ \forall x,\quad x\in L\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \exists y\ \bigl(|y|\le c(|x|+1)^k\ \land\ \langle x,y\rangle\in A\bigr).\]
Here \(c,k\) are integers. The set \(A\) may be assumed to reject malformed pair encodings. The witness bound is a polynomial size bound, not a bound on the cost of finding the witness.

Equivalently, \(L\) has an MA verifier \(W\) that also satisfies
\[\forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^*,\qquad a_W(x,y)\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1].\]
This condition includes witnesses exceeding the chosen length bound; they may be rejected deterministically. It requires one uniform verifier for all \(x,y\), not a separately chosen randomized algorithm for each fixed witness. There is no requirement that a new \(W\) preserve the original verifier's probabilities or use its witness bound.

It follows from these definitions that \(\exists\!\cdot\!\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{MA}\). Thus the substantive equality direction is that every language in MA has some globally gapped witness predicate. A negative answer is a language in MA with no such predicate under any polynomial witness bound. Merely presenting one MA verifier with a probability in the gap does not establish that its language lacks a different globally gapped verifier.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the equality in the uniform, unrelativized language setting. A proof must establish a globally bounded-error witness predicate for every MA language, including exact polynomial runtime and witness-length guarantees. It may change the verifier and witness encoding and need not give an effective conversion between arbitrary machine descriptions. A refutation must prove that some MA language has no existential-BPP representation under any allowed verifier and polynomial bound. One verifier with intermediate acceptance probabilities, or an oracle separation, does not by itself refute the ordinary class equality.

context_blocks.text: Definition 16 applies the existential operator to ordinary languages. Remark 17 explains why fixing a witness in an MA verifier need not leave a BPP computation: a nonwinning witness on a yes-instance may lie inside the error gap. This does not itself prove that the language has no other suitable verifier.

The source encounters this distinction when bounding quantum hierarchies with classical witnesses. Its stronger-oracle simulations handle a different resource class; they do not establish the desired ordinary BPP predicate.

Fenner, Fortnow, Kurtz and Li construct an oracle relative to which MA is not contained even in nondeterministic polynomial time with access to a BPP oracle. Since existential BPP is contained in that latter class, the two target classes can differ relative to a common oracle. This is an obstruction to a proof valid under every oracle, not an unconditional separation.

cards.title: Effective enumeration of BPP
cards.formal:
Does there exist a total computable function \(E\) which, for every index \(i\in\mathbb N\), outputs the finite description of a randomized polynomial-time decision machine \(M_i\), such that
\[\forall i\ \forall x\in\{0,1\}^*,\quad\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\in[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1],\]
and every language in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) is decided by at least one of these machines?

With \(L_i=\{x:\Pr[M_i(x)=1]\ge2/3\}\), the coverage condition is exactly
\[\{L_i:i\in\mathbb N\}=\mathrm{BPP}.\]
Repeated languages and repeated machine descriptions are allowed. The enumeration must include at least one suitable algorithm for each BPP language; it need not list every bounded-error program. There is no efficiency bound on computing \(E(i)\). Each \(M_i\) may have its own polynomial runtime bound, and the enumerator is not additionally required to output that bound.

source_formulation.text: The existence of an effective enumerable family of algorithms deciding all and only the problems in BPP is still an open question.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: Polynomial running time can be guaranteed syntactically by a clock, but bounded error is a condition on every possible input. The question asks whether a computably generated family can still capture all feasible randomized decision problems while guaranteeing that condition. A resolution would clarify the relationship between semantic complexity classes, programming formalisms and what arithmetical theories can certify about randomized computation.
