cards.definitions:
Let \(\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo two. For an integer \(n\ge1\), a matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) defines the total map \(x\mapsto Ax\) from \(\mathbb F_2^n\) to itself, with \((Ax)_i=\bigoplus_{j:a_{ij}=1}x_j\). An empty XOR is zero.

Both types of circuit are finite directed acyclic graphs with distinct input vertices \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and distinct output vertices \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), with the input and output sets disjoint. Inputs have indegree zero and outputs have outdegree zero. Intermediate nodes and output nodes compute functions of their incoming values. Fan-in and fan-out are unrestricted; every edge counts as one wire, including edges into output nodes. Unary gates are permitted. The graph has no parallel edges and there is no depth bound. Size counts wires, not gates, truth-table bits, or the time to evaluate the gates.

In the XOR model every noninput node computes the XOR of all its incoming bits, with a zero-input node computing zero. In the GEN model a noninput node of indegree \(k\) may compute any fixed Boolean function \(\{0,1\}^k\to\{0,1\}\); this includes unary negation, constants and nonlinear functions. Its input wires are ordered when specifying this function. Gate functions and wiring may depend arbitrarily on \(A\), but not on the input vector beyond the values carried by their specified wires. The gate's truth table is not charged; each value transmitted along a wire is one bit. There are no external oracles, advice inputs, random choices, or correctness promises on the input vector.

Write \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) for the respective minimum wire counts of circuits computing every coordinate of \(Ax\) exactly for every \(x\in\mathbb F_2^n\). These finite minima are nonuniform circuit quantities; no efficient algorithm producing an optimum from \(A\) is required. For a nonzero matrix both minima are positive, and \(C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\le C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\) because parity is an allowed general gate. Restricting to nonzero matrices avoids undefined ratios. Arbitrary gates of unbounded fan-in are essential to the source's GEN model; replacing them with a fixed binary Boolean basis would change the question.

The positive constant \(K\) is chosen before the dimension and matrix. They may depend on \(K\), and may be obtained by a nonconstructive argument. A negative answer is exactly a finite constant \(K\) for which \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{GEN}}(A)\) holds for all dimensions and matrices. Computation only on the unit basis vectors is insufficient: nonlinear circuits need not be determined on other inputs by their behavior on that basis.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated unbounded-ratio assertion. A positive answer must establish arbitrarily large wire savings for some matrices, with no prescribed rate or efficient-generation requirement. A negative answer must establish a universal finite simulation factor for every square matrix. A result only for most matrices, for bounded depth, for gates with a bounded arity or fixed basis, or for correctness solely on a selected set of inputs does not settle the claim. A static data-structure lower bound must be shown to imply the exact unrestricted circuit comparison before it can serve as a resolution. No complexity conjecture is assumed.

cards.title: Largest separation between SUM and OR circuits
cards.formal:
Determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the largest possible SUM-over-OR wire-complexity gaps
\[G(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM}}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A)},\qquad
G_2(n)=\max_{A\in\mathcal M_n}\frac{C_{\mathrm{SUM},2}(A)}{C_{\mathrm{OR},2}(A)}.\]
The first ratio allows both circuits arbitrary depth; the second restricts both to the source's two-layer addition model. This retains the two comparisons explicitly motivating Problem 7.1. It compares two ways of evaluating the same zero-one coefficient matrix, not the largest SUM complexity and largest OR complexity on separately chosen matrices.
cards.why: OR can merge repeated contributions while ordinary addition must count each contribution exactly once. The largest possible size difference quantifies how much this idempotence helps when many outputs share partial computations. Separating the unrestricted and depth-two gaps tests how this advantage interacts with the number of computational layers.

cards.title: Unbounded XOR-over-OR complexity separations
cards.formal:
Can XOR wire complexity exceed OR wire complexity by an unbounded factor on the same zero-one matrix? Precisely, is the following statement true?
\[\forall K>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists A\in\mathcal M_n:\quad
C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)>K\,C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A).\]
Both circuit depths are unrestricted. Their outputs use the same coefficient matrix, but OR outputs are Boolean unions and XOR outputs are sums modulo two. No explicitness or efficient matrix-generation condition is imposed. This is the unrestricted ratio question in Problem 7.11, not its depth-two analogue.
cards.why: XOR can cancel duplicate contributions, while OR can merge them. There is no immediate pointwise ordering between the most efficient circuits for these different output semantics. An unbounded gap in this direction would show a systematic limitation of parity computation relative to idempotent merging, even when both can use arbitrary depth.

Every edge counts, including input edges and edges into outputs; gate count and the bit complexity of evaluating an integer sum are not the size measure. Let \(C_L(A)\) be the minimum size for \(L\in\{\mathrm{OR},\mathrm{SUM},\mathrm{XOR}\}\), with depth unrestricted. This is a nonuniform minimum: the circuit can depend arbitrarily on the full matrix, and no efficient construction from its encoding is required. Matrices with nonzero entries have positive complexity. The all-zero matrix is excluded from ratios to avoid \(0/0\).

For the depth-two version \(C_{L,2}(A)\), follow the source's leveled convention: inputs, one intermediate layer, and outputs are three disjoint levels, with edges only from inputs to the intermediate layer or from that layer to outputs. Direct input-to-output edges are not allowed in this version. The intermediate layer may have any finite size; zero outputs and unary gates are allowed. Equivalently, \(C_{L,2}(A)\) minimizes \(|P|+|Q|\) over Boolean matrices \(P\in\{0,1\}^{n\times r}\), \(Q\in\{0,1\}^{r\times n}\), for any integer \(r\ge0\), satisfying \(A=PQ\) over the specified semiring, where \(|P|,|Q|\) count their one-entries. Thus in the SUM case the integer product must have exactly the prescribed zero-one entries, without duplicate contributions.

All these minima exist, and maxima over \(\mathcal M_n\) exist because the matrix set is finite. The extremizing matrices in two different ratios need not be the same. A dimensional asymptotic bound concerns \(n\to\infty\) through all positive integers, with base-two logarithms.

Here \(K\) is any positive real constant and may be replaced by a positive integer without changing the claim. The matrix and its dimension may depend on \(K\). Its negation is the existence of one finite universal \(K\) bounding \(C_{\mathrm{XOR}}(A)\le K C_{\mathrm{OR}}(A)\) at every dimension and every nonzero matrix. Defining \(R(n)\) as the maximum of this ratio makes the question equivalent to unboundedness of \(R\). Appending zero rows and columns preserves both unrestricted minima, so these maxima are nondecreasing; unboundedness is consequently equivalent to \(R(n)\to\infty\). No one finite matrix can by itself show the unbounded assertion.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed quantifiers. A positive answer needs arbitrarily large ratios and may be nonconstructive; it need not attain a specified polynomial rate. A negative answer must supply or establish a uniform finite bound for every matrix. A ratio in the reverse direction, a separation requiring shallow XOR circuits, or a lower bound on the time to rewrite an OR circuit as an XOR circuit does not prove the required unrestricted size separation. Conditional evidence alone does not resolve this unconditional question.

context_blocks.text: The source gives a growing XOR-over-OR gap when both models are restricted to depth two. That lower bound applies to the restricted XOR minimum and need not survive when arbitrary-depth XOR circuits are allowed.

The JCSS paper explicitly reports that it cannot prove a superconstant unrestricted XOR-over-OR gap. Its discussion distinguishes this from the reverse OR-over-XOR direction, where large separations are known. Those reverse-direction matrices do not answer the present quantifiers.

The same paper proves that a truly subquadratic-time general rewriting procedure from OR circuits to XOR circuits would contradict its version of the strong exponential time hypothesis. This concerns computing a new representation, and cannot be substituted for an unconditional size comparison of two optimal representations.

The matrix itself is fixed before either circuit is chosen; treating the two output maps as the same Boolean function would be incorrect. Their common object is the zero-one coefficient pattern, interpreted in two different semirings.

cards.definitions:
A total NP search problem is a polynomial-time decidable relation \(R(a,z)\) with polynomially bounded witnesses z and at least one witness for every input a. A reduction \(R\le S\) consists of deterministic polynomial-time maps F and G such that every S-witness w for \(F(a)\) gives an R-witness \(G(a,w)\); running times are polynomial in the explicit input lengths. For EndOfPotentialLine, an instance consists of circuits \(\mathrm{P},S:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,\ldots ,2^{m}- 1\}\), for \(n,m\ge 1\), with \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}, S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\) and \(V(0^{n})=0\). Potentials are m-bit nonnegative integers. A valid answer is a vertex x satisfying at least one of: \((a) \mathrm{P}(S(x))
e x; (b) x
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(x))
e x; (c) x
e S(x), \mathrm{P}(S(x))=x\) and \(V(S(x))\le V(x)\). UniqueEOPL has the same instances and accepts all these answers, and additionally accepts two vertices \(x
e y\) with \(x
e S(x), y
e S(y)\), and either \(V(x)=V(y)\) or \(V(x)<V(y)<V(S(x))\). Thus uniqueness is enforced by additional verifiable witnesses, not assumed as an unverifiable promise. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with their complete gate lists as input; size includes all gates, wires, input and output labels. The displayed restrictions at \(0^{n}\) are directly checkable; malformed encodings or failed restrictions may be assigned a distinguished trivial answer. EOPL and UEOPL consist of all total NP search problems reducible to their respective canonical problems by the reductions just defined. In particular UEOPL\(\subseteq\)EOPL, since an EndOfPotentialLine answer is always also a UniqueEOPL answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove equality by a polynomial-time reduction from EndOfPotentialLine to UniqueEOPL, valid for every output that the target relation permits, or prove that no such reduction exists. A separation limited to oracle queries or decision trees does not establish inequality of the ordinary circuit-defined classes.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic Turing machine M and fixed positive integers C,k such that on every binary input x, M halts within \(C(|x|+1)^k\) transitions and accepts exactly when x encodes two isomorphic finite simple undirected graphs? Equivalently, is the language \(\mathrm{GI}\) defined below in deterministic polynomial time?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 0\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]\) empty. A finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\) has an adjacency matrix \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) that is symmetric with zero diagonal. Its vertices are labeled; its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Encode a pair G,H by \(1^n0\), followed by the full row-major matrix of G, followed by \(1^m0\) and the full row-major matrix of H. The total binary length is \(N=n^2+m^2+n+m+2\). Extra trailing bits, missing entries, or nonsymmetric or nonzero-diagonal matrices make an encoding malformed. Graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if there is a bijection \(\pi:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(A_G(i,j)=A_H(\pi(i),\pi(j))\) for every \(i,j\in[n]\). If \(n\ne m\), no such bijection exists; the two empty graphs are isomorphic. All valid graph pairs are in the domain, without degree, connectivity, automorphism, sparsity or random-input promises. Computation receives the entire binary string, rather than an oracle or succinctly generated adjacency matrix. The computation model is one uniform classical multitape Turing machine with a finite program, finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. In one transition each tape head moves at most one cell. Time counts all transitions, including input access and internal computation. Polynomial time means a bound \(C(N+1)^k\) for fixed positive integers C,k, independent of the input and of the graph sizes. There is no advice, prover, witness supplied with the input, graph-isomorphism oracle or uncounted preprocessing. The machine is deterministic and must always answer correctly. The language \(\mathrm{GI}\) contains exactly the valid encodings with \(G\cong H\); malformed encodings are rejected. P is the class of all binary languages decided under these uniform deterministic polynomial-time conventions. Ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism is the equivalence relation in the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified language \(\mathrm{GI}\) belongs to P, or that \(\mathrm{GI}\notin\mathrm P\). A positive answer must establish one deterministic machine, fixed polynomial bounds and correctness on every input, including rejection of malformed strings. A negative answer must exclude every such polynomial-time machine; a lower bound for only one algorithm, invariant or representation does not suffice. No isomorphism witness or canonical representative must be output: the target is decision.

context_blocks.text: The same graph can appear under many vertex names. For example, renumbering a cycle leaves its adjacency relations unchanged as an unlabeled structure. Isomorphism asks whether this explains the entire difference between two inputs. A proposed bijection can be checked efficiently, but a negative instance requires ruling out all bijections. This places the decision problem in NP, the class with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable in polynomial time.

Simple summaries can agree on different graphs: a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices and every vertex has degree two. They are not isomorphic because one is connected and the other is disconnected. Any complete decision procedure must distinguish every nonisomorphic pair, including pairs with much stronger coincident invariants.

Babai’s general upper bound has the form \(\exp((\log(n+2))^{O(1)})\). This is a quasipolynomial upper bound, whose permitted exponents go beyond the fixed polynomial bound requested here. It does not prove a superpolynomial lower bound on the problem or on every implementation of that method.

Efficient algorithms on restricted graph classes provide substantial structure without settling the unrestricted target. In particular, a runtime with a degree or width parameter in the exponent is polynomial when that parameter is fixed, but it need not be polynomial when the parameter grows with the input. The 2026 survey explicitly separates these parameterized bounds from the general open problem.

A randomized polynomial-time algorithm with bounded error for ordinary isomorphism would settle the neighboring BPP question. It would not by itself provide the deterministic algorithm asked for here. A quantum algorithm deciding the same ordinary relation is another computational variant; the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism is a different mathematical target.

The two consolidated MFCS 2021 sources independently restate the general polynomial-time question. Butti and Dalmau discuss it beside fractional homomorphisms and linear-programming relaxations. Dawar and Vagnozzi discuss its equivalence to computing automorphism-orbit partitions and compare algebraic relaxations. These source contexts are preserved without substituting a conjecture about one relaxation for general graph isomorphism.
